On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.","feed_description":"Using verified task outcomes to guide dense teacher feedback helps language models learn mathematical reasoning more effectively from student-generated responses.","pdf_only":false,"paper_summary":{"summary":"The authors introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD) for mathematical reasoning, using teacher–verifier agreement within groups of sampled responses to scale teacher guidance across next-token choices. VOPD compares teacher preferences with verified outcomes through a reference-model log-probability shift. In tests of two Qwen3 configurations and eight math benchmarks, it averages 66.38, above OPD and ExOPD, using the student’s top 16 tokens.","feedDescription":"Using verified task outcomes to guide dense teacher feedback helps language models learn mathematical reasoning more effectively from student-generated responses.","originalProblem":["Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards provides outcome-grounded feedback, but its response-level rewards are sparse and updates focus on sampled actions.","On-policy distillation provides dense teacher guidance across next-token choices, but the teacher’s preferences may not match which responses a verifier judges correct.","Simply combining distillation and verifier-based policy updates does not directly use verifier outcomes to adjust the teacher’s token-level guidance."],"solution":["For each prompt, sample a group of student responses and compare their verifier scores with their cumulative teacher-versus-reference log-probability rewards.","Estimate the within-group correlation between verifier outcomes and teacher preference; use its sign and magnitude to scale or reverse the teacher-directed update.","Convert the adjusted signal into dense next-token supervision by taking an expectation over the student’s token distribution, alongside the standard reverse-KL distillation objective."],"keyInsights":["Verifier feedback can modify distillation through a prompt-specific estimate of teacher–verifier alignment, rather than through a separate policy-gradient signal alone.","Positive alignment extrapolates beyond the teacher in the teacher–reference direction; negative alignment moves supervision back toward the reference policy.","Alignment varies substantially across prompts, and zero-variance verifier groups are frequent with groups of four responses, motivating adaptive rather than fixed-strength adjustment."],"results":["On eight math benchmarks, VOPD averaged 66.38 accuracy for same-size distillation, versus 64.71 for standard OPD, 64.75 for OPD+GRPO, and 65.25 for fixed-strength ExOPD; How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs N recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes N ) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with N = 2 and N = 4 match the no-sleep baseline’s loss using 2.10× and 2.39× fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.","feed_description":"Periodic offline refinement of a language model’s context cache helps it learn from examples with fewer tokens, without slowing token generation between refinement steps.","pdf_only":false,"paper_summary":{"summary":"Sleep lets Transformer models refine their key-value cache at chunk boundaries, using recurrent passes over context already read. Rather than add depth to every generated token, the model updates its attention memory periodically, then resumes ordinary decoding. On held-out code, 1.2B-parameter models matched baseline loss with 2.10× fewer context tokens at N=2 and 2.39× at N=4; this measures prefix length, not speed.","feedDescription":"Periodic offline Student @ Brown University","bio":"Enyan Zhang’s Instilling Inductive Biases with Subnetworks utilizes specialized model components to introduce specific computational biases into neural networks. Zhang is a PhD student at Yale University working with Professor Tom McCoy on NLP and the interpretation of neural networks as models of language and cognition.
